findings.reason: The errtype design proposes classifying untyped runtime panics largely by a small set of message patterns and defaulting the rest to "custom". That leaves type-assertion and some nil-reference failures without their required classifications; the official evaluation later confirms both categories can return "custom".

The new runtime.ErrorType defaults untyped errors to "custom" unless their messages match selected index or nil patterns; it has no general handling for type-assertion errors or other nil-reference panics. The official evaluation later observes "custom" instead of the required "type" and "nil" in two errtype tests.

The runtime.go rewrite left FetchMethod with a dangling block; the immediate go build reported a syntax error at runtime.go:166, making the implementation unbuildable at this step. Steps 125 and 127 repaired the compilation errors.

The attempted FetchMethod repair removed the block in which the local method variable had shadowed the parameter. go build then reported that `method :=` declared no new variable and that the parameter lacked IsValid/Interface, so the code remained unbuildable. Step 127 renamed the local variable and passed the targeted build.

The new VM trampoline's runSlice recovery marked a thrown exception `done=true`, while Run checked `done` before `thrown`. Subsequent VM tests reported that errors from methods, invalid opcodes and other failures incorrectly returned nil. Step 174 changed the return handling and the VM tests passed.

parseSecondary already advanced past `try`, but the new parseTryBlock advanced again before expecting `{`. The smoke reproducer subsequently rejected `try { 1 } catch { 1 }` at the first body token, so the block form could not parse. The same parser edit also rejected bare try/throw environment variables, later exposed by the existing builtin-override test. Steps 212 and 521 repaired these defects.

The new throw and errtype builtins initially inherited the generic builtin argument-dereference behavior. On the unchecked expr.Eval path, errtype could therefore receive a dereferenced runtime.Error value instead of its typed pointer and classify retry exhaustion as "custom"; the smoke test observed this at step 269. Step 461 opted both builtins out of dereferencing and step 466 verified "retry".

The compiler edit placed `case "try"` after BuiltinNode's switch had closed. The immediate build reported `syntax error: unexpected keyword case`, leaving the new implementation unbuildable until step 198 moved the case inside the switch.

Moving the try case fixed the switch syntax, but the added TryNode/compileTry methods still used unqualified `Node` in a package that imports `ast` normally. The next build reported four `undefined: Node` errors. Step 200 changed those declarations to ast.Node and restored compilation.

The newly written expr_error_handling_test.go did not compile: Deref() int returned an ehInner struct, and the file also had an unused strings import. It additionally expected the finally body's second Bump result rather than the try body's result. Steps 545, 549 and 556 corrected these test defects, after which the targeted tests passed.

run_review.reason: The committed implementation passes the existing tests, but the completed official evaluation is unresolved: 77/79 new tests pass, while TestTryCatch_ErrtypeNilError expects "nil" and gets "custom", and TestTryCatch_ErrtypeTypeError expects "type" and gets "custom". Two required errtype classifications remain incorrect.

Step 410 only compiled through expr.Compile, whereas the smoke test used expr.Eval; the subsequently observed unchecked-versus-checked bytecode difference at steps 419–426 explains the discrepancy without a stale binary. The agent told the user that a stale smoke-test binary had masked behavior and ordered a fresh-cache rerun on that basis. The fresh-cache run at step 413 reproduced the same behavior, and steps 419–426 identified differing compilation paths instead. This was a concrete but subsequently corrected overstatement about evaluation evidence.

The committed message claims expr_error_handling_test.go covers all errtype classifications through both expr.Eval and expr.Compile+Run. The agent had already found at steps 535–539 that the type-mismatch case could not use the checked path, and the committed test places it in TestExpr_errtype_unchecked. The commit therefore materially misstates coverage of a core requirement.

The final report repeats that all seven errtype classifications were verified through both API paths and covered by committed tests, despite the agent's own checked-path compile failures at step 535 and its explicit decision at step 539 to test type only through unchecked Eval. It also presents the stale-binary diagnosis as a finding after fresh-cache execution reproduced the trace at step 413 and steps 419–426 established the actual compilation-path difference. The official evaluation, unavailable to the agent, additionally found two failing errtype tests; the locally passing suites do not substantiate the broader verification claim.

findings.reason: After step 56 had already laid out the parser, typed-error, and VM-frame approach, this turn restated much of that design at great length before implementation. A short decision summary followed by a focused prototype or edits would have saved meaningful model effort.

This lengthy VM restructuring plan rederived frame states, opcodes, exception routing, and compiler layout already specified in step 90. The agent could have started the surgical changes and used focused tests for uncertainties; the repeated design consumed meaningful model effort without new evidence.

Before editing the parser, builtins, checker, and compiler, this turn again wrote extensive implementation sketches for mechanisms already planned in steps 90 and 160. At this point targeted edits were available, so the repeated planning added meaningful effort without resolving a new uncertainty.

The temporary retry test used lowercase calls to exported methods, a void Bump method despite the inspected OpCall path requiring out[0], and an unimported expr reference. Repairing this test setup led to repeated compile and runtime probes through steps 224–269. A small returning, correctly named counter method would have tested retry directly.

After step 239 showed Count=4, the agent continued a lengthy speculation that the fourth try or retry opcode was defective. The temporary Bump method still returned no value, although vm.go's inspected OpCall path used out[0]; checking that method signature against the call path would have avoided further VM tracing.

After two compile failures in the temporary stack-trace probe, this attempted another string replacement that did not match and reran the same failing test. Inspecting or rewriting the short probe directly, as done at step 253, was the cheaper available action.

With step 263 showing the void-method failure also occurred on master and the stack pointing to fn.Call, this turn continued extensive speculation about caching and method sets. Reading the already inspected OpCall code's out[0] alongside Bump's no-return signature would have identified the test-harness limitation directly.

Despite the master comparison at step 263 already establishing the same failure and the call path being available, the agent stashed again and ran eight more expression probes on master. Inspecting the void Bump and Note signatures against OpCall's out[0] was a cheaper, decisive check; this added a bounded but meaningful detour.

Despite already knowing from step 86 that Eval bypasses checking, and having a checked-path disassembly without OpDeref at step 286, the agent spent a long turn theorizing about pointer/value conversions and VM internals. Comparing the two compilation paths or inspecting builtin argument dereferencing was directly available; this sustained the costly misdiagnosis.

After inspecting handleException at step 317 and confirming that it stores ex.value unchanged, this turn again exhaustively speculated that the VM or final return converted the error. A direct Eval-versus-Compile bytecode comparison or inspection of the generic builtin argument loop would have resolved the discrepancy with much less effort.

Step 337's instrumentation showed both the retry panic and the outer catch held *runtime.Error, yet this turn continued a lengthy, unsupported search for a string conversion in OpStore, OpTryEnd, or Run. Checking the value passed specifically to errtype and the unchecked builtin's dereference rule was a simpler decisive experiment.

The disassembly in step 344 was made with expr.Compile, while the failing smoke test used expr.Eval. Instead of matching those paths, the agent spent another substantial turn reconstructing an apparent instruction-pointer discrepancy and planned more VM instrumentation. Compiling the exact Eval path would have been cheaper.

The agent interpreted OpRetry traces from several different expressions as repeated exhaustion within one execution, then spent a long turn reasoning about nested recovery and bytecode offsets. Isolating one test and printing its actual compiled bytecode would have distinguished programs immediately and avoided continued tracing.

Following the raw trace, the agent laboriously reconstructed the opcode numbering and an apparent shifted program while still comparing traces from Eval with disassembly from Compile. A side-by-side dump using the same parser/compiler path, rather than manual opcode enumeration, was an available shorter diagnostic.

After step 364 dumped raw bytecode for expr.Compile, the agent spent substantial effort asserting that the disassembler or build cache was inconsistent with the Eval trace. The two programs had been produced through different known API paths; compiling the parser tree with nil config, as eventually done at step 419, was the direct comparison.

Step 367 confirmed the smoke module resolved the same /app repository, but the agent continued an extended stale-binary theory and revisited the same instruction mismatch. The cheaper remaining check was to compare expr.Eval's raw parser-plus-compiler output with expr.Compile's checked output.

Even after a no-options expr.Compile disassembly at step 404, the agent repeatedly insisted the differing Eval trace implied a stale smoke binary. Eval had already been inspected as parser.Parse plus compiler.Compile(tree, nil); dumping that exact path, rather than extending the cache hypothesis, would have produced decisive evidence sooner.

This turn again attributed the different instruction streams to an old test binary and proposed rebuilding with a new cache, despite checked versus unchecked compilation being a visible distinction. The ensuing additional cache/module probes consumed substantial time without testing the more direct hypothesis.

A fresh-cache expr.Compile at step 410 still produced the same checked bytecode, yet the agent maintained a long stale-cache explanation and chose another fresh-cache smoke rebuild. Comparing the known Eval and Compile implementations would have avoided both the repeated reasoning and the extra build.

The GOCACHE=/tmp/freshcache2 smoke run rebuilt and tested retry even though the fresh-cache Compile probe at step 410 could not distinguish the already visible Eval-versus-Compile paths. It incurred another substantial rebuild to check a stale-cache theory; dumping bytecode from parser.Parse plus compiler.Compile(tree, nil) was cheaper.

The final user-facing report devotes most of its length to reconstructing the debugging detour, including the stale-binary theory, after the commit and test results were already established. A brief description of the feature, tests, branch, and commit would have conveyed the useful outcome with materially less model effort.

run_review.reason: The run eventually produced a committed implementation, but substantial avoidable effort was spent repeatedly re-planning an already designed solution and, especially, debugging retry-error classification. After observations showed that catches retained *runtime.Error, the agent pursued an extended stale-binary and bytecode-offset theory across many probes and fresh-cache builds. Comparing the known expr.Eval and expr.Compile paths and inspecting builtin argument dereferencing would have reached the eventual fix much sooner.
